endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Document how Risk Assessment is evaluated, recorded, retained, and reviewed.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: This element also considers accurate tool use and recognition of erroneous tool outputs, compliance with human-oversight checkpoints before irreversible or high-consequence actions, graceful handling of tool failures, and resistance to prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved content, and tool outputs.

endorsements.title: Chinese expert concern and consensus on applications of artificial intelligence in clinical cancer imaging
endorsements.quote: AI models used in surgical navigation or intelligent surgical assistance systems should undergo thorough validation of safety, accuracy, and stability prior to clinical deployment.

evidence.title: PhysicianBench: Evaluating LLM Agents in Real-World EHR Environments
evidence.outcome: Agent success rate on long-horizon EHR tasks requiring tool use, multi-step planning, and consequential actions
evidence.effect: Best model reached 46% pass@1; open-source models reached at most 19%, across 100 tasks averaging 27 tool calls.
evidence.quote: Across 13 proprietary and open-source LLM agents, the best-performing model achieves only 46% success rate (pass@1), while open-source models reach at most 19%, revealing a substantial gap between current agent capabilities and the demands of real-world clinical workflows.

evidence.title: HealthCraft: A Reinforcement Learning Safety Environment for Emergency Medicine
evidence.outcome: Agent performance on multi-step emergency medicine workflows with tool use
evidence.effect: Multi-step workflow performance collapsed to near zero (Claude 1.0%, GPT-5.4 0.0%) despite partial competence on individual steps; safety-failure rates were 27.5% and 34.0% overall.
evidence.quote: On multi-step workflows - the closest proxy to real emergency care - performance collapses to near zero (Claude 1.0%, GPT-5.4 0.0%) despite partial competence on individual steps.

evidence.title: Asclepius: An Adaptive Harness for Long-Horizon Clinical Agents
evidence.outcome: Agent completeness and timeliness of critical actions in simulated ED shift
evidence.effect: Current agents reach correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap.
evidence.quote: On CES, current agents reach the correct diagnosis in most cases yet fail to deliver complete and timely critical actions, revealing an execution gap.

evidence.title: SkinAgent AI: A Safety-Grounded Multimodal Agentic Framework for Non-Diagnostic Skincare Support
evidence.outcome: Agent tool selection, task completion, and failure fallback on a locked benchmark
evidence.effect: Exact tool-set match 62.92%, strict task completion 47.08%, intent accuracy 80.00%; tool-selection errors and unreliable failure fallback remained.
evidence.quote: Tool-selection errors, incomplete grounding of product attributes, and unreliable failure fallback nevertheless remained.

evidence.title: Clinical agents fail silently on patient identity
evidence.outcome: Agent withholding writes on tampered patient-identity visits (tamper detection)
evidence.effect: GPT-4.1 withheld writing in 17.4% of header-swap runs; detection of MRN or age changes near zero. GPT-4.1-nano detected 4.4% of header swaps and <1% of MRN/age changes.
evidence.quote: Agents usually copied codes into tampered charts.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether dry-run evaluation of agentic AI before enabling high-impact actions reduces erroneous or irreversible actions. Five benchmark studies show that current agents often fail multi-step tool tasks and failure handling, which suggests the hazard is real but leaves the safeguard's value unmeasured.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The five supplied studies are automated benchmarks that document the hazard in simulated or offline settings. They show that agents fail, but they do not compare deployment with and without dry-run testing, so they cannot show that the safeguard prevents harm.

In emergency medicine workflows, multi-step performance fell to 1.0% and 0.0%, with safety-failure rates of 27.5% and 34.0%. GPT-4.1 withheld writes in 17.4% of tampered-identity runs and rarely detected MRN or age changes. A dry run might expose these failure modes before an action reaches a patient record, though no study confirms this.

On 100 EHR tasks averaging 27 tool calls, the best model passed 46% on first attempt and open-source models passed at most 19%. A locked benchmark found 47.08% strict task completion with unreliable failure fallback. A simulated ED shift found correct diagnoses but incomplete and late actions. No study measured the staff time a dry-run program would require.

A regulatory discussion paper describes evaluating tool use, human-oversight checkpoints before irreversible actions, and handling of tool failures. CHAI playbooks require documented risk assessment, and a Chinese consensus calls for validating surgical AI before deployment. These sources treat pre-deployment testing as expected conduct, but none cites outcome data showing that such testing reduces harm.

None of the hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two do not report a setting. Benchmark tasks may not reflect records with interpreter notes, fragmented care, or identity mismatches, which may occur more often in safety-net systems.

Agents in one benchmark rarely noticed when a patient's MRN or age had been changed, so a wrong-patient write could proceed without a person seeing it. Patients may reasonably expect that a human reviews any irreversible action taken in their record.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares agents deployed after dry-run evaluation with agents deployed without it, or measures whether dry-run findings predict erroneous or irreversible actions in live use. Studies in live or shadow-mode clinical settings should report reversal rates, near misses, and staff time.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the hazard studies included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether agent failure rates, or any benefit of dry-run testing, differ for their patients.
